facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest case against the low-leverage reading is that FY2026 earnings look unusually good for a commodity cooperative. Energy earned USD 554.6 million of pre-tax earnings after a USD 19.0 million loss in FY2025, helped by about USD 205.0 million of small refinery exemption relief, and record renewable energy credit costs were largely offset by higher crack spreads and wider crude oil discounts. If EBITDA returned to the FY2025 level of USD 1,412.3 million, FY2026 year-end total debt would be 1.77x and the February 2026 quarter-end total debt of USD 4,127.8 million would be 2.92x. The view would turn if period-end debt stays near its February level after the fiscal 2027 capital programme starts, if equity distributions from CF Nitrogen fall, or if the covenant levels, which the filings do not give, prove tight against those ratios. Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 67; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 64; calculation C02; calculation C25; calculation C26

facts.label: Contrary evidence and what would change the view
facts.text: The strongest evidence against a cautious reading is that even the downside case leaves net debt at 3.26x EBITDA at the seasonal peak, committed lines of USD 2,800.0 million exceed the USD 725.5 million of extra borrowing it needs, and member equity of USD 11,644.8 million is 57.90% of assets, so a liquidity break would need a worse outcome than a repeat of FY2025. The view would improve if covenant levels show wide headroom, if period-end debt stays well below the February level, or if Energy earnings prove less dependent on exemptions. It would worsen if the securitization and repurchase facilities are not extended beyond August 25, 2027, if equity distributions from CF Nitrogen fall while capital spending runs at USD 850.8 million, or if payouts exceed the USD 300.0 million intended. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation B09; calculation B15

facts.label: Strengths and weaknesses
facts.text: CHS's main strengths are financial, not competitive. Low year-end leverage and high interest cover let it absorb one weak year without refinancing pressure, as net debt of 1.14x EBITDA and cover of 11.79x show. A USD 2,800.0 million undrawn committed revolver and a long-dated unsecured note stack mean no large maturity wall, with USD 450.0 million the largest year. Member equity of 57.90% of assets and board-discretionary redemption of equity certificates give a buffer. Scale, with USD 39.2 billion of revenue across energy, grains and crop inputs, spreads exposure across three commodity chains. Finally, there is no sponsor, so value extraction by an owner is not a documented risk. facts.label: Company description and group structure
facts.text: CHS is a farmer-owned cooperative whose three reportable segments run on commodity spreads. Energy refines about 190,000 barrels a day at Laurel and McPherson, Grains is the largest cooperative marketer and processor of grain and oilseeds, and Agronomy sells crop inputs and holds a 7.86% interest in CF Nitrogen. Revenue is price-driven and thin-margin, so the cash that services debt comes from refining spreads, processing margins and joint venture distributions, not from revenue scale. Grains is 55.02% of revenue but 11.29% of pre-tax earnings, while Energy is 28.96% of revenue and 49.13% of earnings. Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 67

facts.text: Cash conversion swings with working capital and capital spending. facts.label: Competitive forces and policy environment
facts.text: Rivalry and buyer power cap pricing. CHS competes with larger, better known companies, its members are not obliged to trade with it, and consolidation among cooperative customers and input manufacturers could remove it from supply chains. Substitution matters mainly to Energy, where lower fuel demand would hit diesel sold to farms. These forces explain why margins are thin and why creditors should not extrapolate FY2026 spreads, but they also spread risk across many customers, none above 10% of receivables. Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 28–30; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 153

facts.label: SWOT in credit terms
facts.text: Strengths: low year-end leverage, large unsecured term debt with no large maturity wall, USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver, member equity buffer and board-controlled payouts. Weaknesses: thin margins, half of pre-tax earnings from joint ventures, policy-dependent Energy earnings, seasonal debt and unknown covenants. Opportunities: the Wisconsin soybean plant and phosphate venture could add earnings from late 2028 or 2029 if approved and funded sensibly, and lower major maintenance in fiscal 2027 helps cash. Threats: a repeat of FY2025 margins, loss of CF Nitrogen distributions, non-renewal of the receivables facilities by August 2027, farm credit losses at CHS Capital, and tax or exemption changes. facts.label: Financial profile and credit quality
facts.text: Scale and market position are strong: revenue of USD 39.2 billion and a leading cooperative position in energy and grains. Competitive advantage is average, resting on member relationships and owned logistics rather than pricing power. Business diversification is average because three chains are diversified but equity income concentrates earnings in one joint venture. Cost and capex flexibility is average, since payouts and growth capital are discretionary while refineries need turnarounds. Margin stability is weak, with gross margin at 3.21% in FY2025 and 4.56% in FY2026. Free cash flow stability is average, from minus USD 364.2 million to USD 1,052.5 million. Ability to refinance is average: long-dated unsecured notes show private market access, but no rating or market data is supplied and the receivables lines renew in 2027. Liquidity is strong at the year end with USD 3,063.6 million of cash and undrawn revolver, subject to unstated letters of credit. Financial policy and governance is average: no sponsor and board control support creditors, but payouts are discretionary and covenants are unseen. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation B05; calculation B11; calculation B12

facts.text: Over twelve to twenty-four months, tailwinds are the company's FY2026 operating cash flow, lower major maintenance of USD 41.8 million, higher crush margins from biofuel policy and CF Nitrogen pricing, while headwinds are weak farm demand, record renewable credit costs, a possible end to exemptions and capital spending of USD 850.8 million. facts.label: Downside scenario
facts.text: The downside is a repeat of FY2025 conditions at peak-season borrowing under the fiscal 2027 plan. The initiating condition is Energy margins falling back as crack spreads and exemptions normalise while farmers defer purchases and trade restrictions persist. The first operating break is Energy and Agronomy earnings; operating cash flow falls to the FY2025 level of USD 635.8 million against USD 1,361.3 million of planned capital spending, major maintenance, preferred dividends and member payouts, a shortfall of USD 725.5 million that is funded by borrowing. Net debt would then be about USD 2,963.6 million at year end, 2.10x FY2025-level EBITDA of USD 1,412.3 million, and about USD 4,604.8 million at the seasonal peak, 3.26x. The revolver of USD 2,800.0 million exceeds the extra borrowing, so liquidity would hold, and the observable triggers are covenant tests, the August 2027 receivables renewal and the April 2028 revolver expiry. Management levers are lower payouts and capital spending, which the board has used before. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation B08; calculation B09; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 76; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 163–164

facts.label: Overall credit view
facts.text: Overall, CHS presents a strong business profile on scale and a cooperative structure with no sponsor, but credit quality is constrained by thin and policy-dependent margins, half of pre-tax earnings from joint ventures and seasonal debt that is far above the year-end level. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: cover is high in a good year but free cash flow was negative in FY2025. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on renewing the receivables facilities by August 2027 and the revolver by April 2028 and on covenant headroom that the filings do not show. The primary downside path is a margin downturn that meets peak-season borrowing while payouts and capital spending rise. Further analysis would require the credit agreement, covenant levels, ratings and CHS Capital loan data. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: policy-dependent Energy margins meeting peak-season borrowing. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)

## Findings
### Bottom line

The seven supplied filings and releases are enough to run the Financial foundation, Business & governance and Fundamental credit work on CHS INC, but they cannot support any covenant level, rating or letter-of-credit conclusion.

Creditors should read headroom statements as unverified, because the filings say only that minimum consolidated net worth and other financial ratios apply and that the company was in compliance. The fourth quarter must be derived from the annual report less nine months, because no standalone fourth-quarter statements were supplied.

spans.text: # CP-1 Financial foundation for CHS INC (chscp), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Financial foundation for CHS INC (issuer id chscp), as of 2026-11-05, on the credit_snapshot pathway. Scope: statements, debt, liquidity, leverage and coverage built from the seven supplied filings and releases, with every figure traced to its page.
## Sources

| 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl | Annual report on Form 10-K of CHS Inc. for the fiscal year ended August 31, 2026, with audited consolidated statements and notes | 2026-11-04 | 7af90f68bff1cc427159bcc12ffc87c427ce829f2621b0c4238922f45880492c | Date taken from the signature page; statements, debt note, liquidity, equities, segments, cash flow and contractual obligations |

| 10-Q_2025-11-30_chscp-20251130.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended November 30, 2025 | 2026-01-07 | 3b343d46b4f667e29be99b08f7d799dc25471f06dbcbf91d62c596b40053bc50 | Date taken from the signature page; period-end balance sheet, debt and facility usage at November 30, 2025 |

| 10-Q_2026-02-28_chscp-20260228.htm.jsonl | Quarterly report on Form 10-Q for the quarter ended February 28, 2026 | 2026-04-08 | 335ab8ab1983479e957ab5bcc688bac42f2a8847cb6800ad1d72a83671457084 | Date taken from the signature page; period-end balance sheet, debt and facility usage at February 28, 2026 |

| EX-99.1_2026-07-08_a3qfy26earningrelease.htm.jsonl | Press release on third quarter fiscal year 2026 earnings (Exhibit 99.1) | 2026-07-08 | 9732954cd83cfd2faab08d34c8a937435e86ab588c7e99ee653b9179d1961e0c | Nine-month segment earnings used to derive fourth-quarter segment earnings |

| EX-99.1_2026-11-04_a4qfy26earningrelease.htm.jsonl | Press release on fiscal year 2026 earnings (Exhibit 99.1) | 2026-11-04 | cae53d4e6b095242a55a168a21c6d1a5d0c45880ba1e0b3a388701114a691f44 | Full-year segment earnings and fiscal 2027 distribution intent |
| Handoff | Module | sha256 | Use |
| Source readiness | CP-0 | 65d7ae926eea08b1a1d51b5c839edac351dde3a8b8008dba76723e1db5de6107 | Source set, gaps and the conflict on the second quarter release label |
## Findings
### Bottom line

CHS carries low leverage at its August 31, 2026 year end, with net debt of USD 2,238.1 million at 1.14x EBITDA, but that is the seasonal low and 28.9% of the EBITDA is equity income, so creditors should underwrite to seasonal-high debt.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 144; 10-Q_2026-02-28_chscp-20260228.htm.jsonl, page 4; calculation C07; calculation C20

CHS reports no EBITDA, so the figure used is net income plus interest, tax and depreciation and amortisation. Net debt was USD 3,879.3 million at the February 28, 2026 quarter end, the highest period-end balance in the sources and 1.73 times the year-end level, and Q4 alone produced 65.5% of annual pre-tax earnings.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 144–146; calculation C01; calculation C18; calculation C22
### Key findings

- Year-end leverage is low and falling, but it is a seasonal low. Total debt was USD 2,501.7 million at the 2026 year end, 1.27x EBITDA, against 2.12x a year earlier, while the working-capital lines swelled debt to a February quarter-end high. A lender sizing to that high sees 1.73 times the year-end net debt, so the year-end ratio overstates the cushion.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 144; 10-Q_2026-02-28_chscp-20260228.htm.jsonl, page 4; calculation C04; calculation C17; calculation C18

- The EBITDA behind that leverage is a house calculation and 28.9% of it is equity income from joint ventures. Distributions from investees exceeded equity income by USD 25.4 million in FY2026, and CF Nitrogen alone paid USD 447.3 million, so the income was cash-backed this year, but it depends on urea and UAN prices. On EBITDA excluding equity income and other income, FY2026 total debt is 1.97x.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 146; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 158; calculation C01; calculation C19; calculation C20

- Earnings are back-ended. Q4 pre-tax earnings were USD 739.3 million, 65.5% of the year, after a nine-month operating loss. The annual report's own seasonality table shows Q4 at a much lower share and Q2 as a positive share although Q2 was a loss, so seasonality should be read from the quarterly filings, not from that table.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 60; 10-Q_2026-05-31_chscp-20260531.htm.jsonl, page 5; calculation C22

- Cash generation was strong but concentrated in Q4. Operating cash flow was USD 1,584.0 million, of which USD 1,382.8 million came in Q4 as receivables unwound and earnings peaked; free cash flow after capital spending and major maintenance was USD 1,052.5 million, and USD 753.4 million after preferred dividends, patronage cash and equity redemptions.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 146; 10-Q_2026-05-31_chscp-20260531.htm.jsonl, pages 5–6; calculation C23; calculation C24

- Coverage is ample. EBITDA covered cash interest paid 11.79x in FY2026 against 9.57x in FY2025, even though interest expense rose USD 17.6 million on a higher average short-term balance and less capitalised interest.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 146; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 72–73; calculation C13

- Liquidity rests on a committed revolver and the securitization lines. At year end the USD 2,800.0 million revolver was undrawn alongside USD 263.6 million of cash. The securitization and repurchase facilities, which reached USD 850.0 million and USD 250.0 million of use at quarter ends, run only to August 25, 2027, and letters of credit under the revolver are not stated, so availability net of them is not established.

- The debt stack is long-dated and unsecured where it is term debt: USD 1,703.0 million of private placement notes and a USD 300.0 million term loan, with USD 450.0 million due in fiscal 2030 as the largest single year. The maturity chart also counts the short-term notes payable in fiscal 2027, so that bar is a rollover need, not scheduled amortisation.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 164–165; calculation C09

- Claims on cash are rising. Capital expenditures are expected at USD 850.8 million in FY2027 against USD 463.3 million in FY2026, and the company intends USD 300.0 million of patronage cash and equity redemptions beside USD 168.7 million of preferred dividends. Counting the USD 2,264.0 million of preferred stock as debt-like lifts FY2026 net leverage to 2.29x.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 76; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_a4qfy26earningrelease.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation C21
### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest case against the low-leverage reading is that FY2026 earnings look unusually good for a commodity cooperative. Energy earned USD 554.6 million of pre-tax earnings after a USD 19.0 million loss in FY2025, helped by about USD 205.0 million of small refinery exemption relief, and record renewable energy credit costs were largely offset by higher crack spreads and wider crude oil discounts. If EBITDA returned to the FY2025 level of USD 1,412.3 million, FY2026 year-end total debt would be 1.77x and the February 2026 quarter-end total debt of USD 4,127.8 million would be 2.92x. The view would turn if period-end debt stays near its February level after the fiscal 2027 capital programme starts, if equity distributions from CF Nitrogen fall, or if the covenant levels, which the filings do not give, prove tight against those ratios.

### Limitations

- The company reports no EBITDA, so every leverage and coverage ratio uses a house calculation that includes equity income; on the narrower operating definition the ratios are higher, and the low-leverage conclusion is weaker.
- Covenant levels are not stated, so headroom is not established and the conclusion cannot be tested against the tests that bind.
- The August 31, 2024 balance sheet and the fiscal 2025 annual report are not in the sources, so FY2024 leverage is not established and the FY2025 revolver size rests on the first-quarter report.

- CHS Capital, the financing subsidiary, discloses no separate cash, EBITDA or cash flow, so industrial leverage is not established; its notes payable of USD 255.4 million are matched-funding debt that cannot be set against industrial EBITDA.
- The legal ranking, guarantors and call terms of the notes are not stated, so no debt stack is drawn and the structural position of unsecured creditors is not established.
- Q4 figures are derived by subtracting unaudited nine-month statements from the audited year, so quarterly conclusions inherit any difference between the two sets.

## Gaps

- The August 31, 2024 balance sheet is not in the sources, so total debt, cash, net debt and leverage for FY2024 are not established; this restricts the leverage trend to two year ends. Severity Medium. Supplying the fiscal 2025 annual report would close it.

- Covenant levels and definitions for minimum consolidated net worth and the other financial ratios are not stated, so headroom cannot be calculated for any period. Severity High. Supplying the credit agreement and a compliance certificate would close it.

- The company states no EBITDA or adjusted EBITDA, so EBITDA is calculated from net income, interest, tax and depreciation and amortization for FY2026, FY2025 and FY2024, and no EBITDA bridge or issuer-adjusted ratios can be given. Severity Medium. A management EBITDA definition would close it.

- The legal rank, guarantors and obligor scope of the notes, term loan, revolver and securitization are not stated, so the debt stack is not drawn. Severity Medium. Supplying the executed debt documents would close it.
- Letters of credit issued under the revolver are not stated, so undrawn availability for FY2026 and FY2025 is gross of any. Severity Medium. A facility usage statement would close it.

- The size of the revolver at August 31, 2025 is taken from the first-quarter report, because the fiscal 2025 annual report is not in the sources, so FY2025 undrawn capacity rests on that report. Severity Low. The fiscal 2025 annual report would close it.

- CHS Capital cash, EBITDA, operating cash flow, capital spending and liquidity are not disclosed separately, so industrial and finance leverage are not split; its notes payable of USD 255.4 million sit inside total debt. Severity Medium. CHS Capital stand-alone statements would close it.

- Per-note carrying values, call terms and amortisation of the private placement notes are not stated; carrying value is shown at principal with one financing cost adjustment. Severity Low. The note purchase agreements would close it.

- Q4 FY2026 and Q4 FY2025 are not reported on their own and are derived by subtracting unaudited nine-month figures from the annual figures; segment pre-tax earnings for Q4 rest on the same subtraction. Severity Low. A fourth-quarter statement set would close it.

- The annual report's quarterly seasonality table for FY2026 prints Q2 at 15% and Q4 at 36%, which the quarterly filings contradict; the derived shares are used. Severity Low. A corrected table would close it.

- Interim last-twelve-months EBITDA is not constructed, so leverage at the February peak is shown only as net debt and as a multiple of year-end net debt and of FY2025 EBITDA. Severity Low. Not needed for the year-end view.

- The fiscal 2027 maturity bar includes short-term notes payable of 449.002 that are renewed rather than scheduled to amortise, which overstates scheduled repayments. Severity Low. Management's expected refinancing plan would close it.

## Findings
### Bottom line

CHS is a member-owned cooperative with no sponsor to extract value, so creditor governance risk is moderate and comes from discretionary member payouts, USD 2,264.0 million of preferred stock and 50.4% of pre-tax earnings being equity income.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 91; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 144; calculation A04; Source readiness (CP-0)

Directors are farmer-elected by region, no employee may sit on the board, and preferred holders and lenders have no vote. Cash patronage and equity redemptions paid fell to USD 130.4 million in FY2026 from USD 721.9 million in FY2024, but the company intends USD 300.0 million in fiscal 2027 while capital spending is guided to USD 850.8 million.

Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 91–92; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 146; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_a4qfy26earningrelease.htm.jsonl, page 1; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 76; calculation A05
### Key findings

- No sponsor controls CHS, so the usual extraction risk is absent, but control sits with member-elected directors and creditors have no vote. Voting rights arise from membership rather than from equity or debt, the bylaws bar employees from the board, and the board has seventeen seats with one vacant, so the discipline on payouts rests on the board's policy and on debt terms the filings do not show.

- Member distributions are the financial-policy lever and the board sets them at its discretion. Cash patronage and equity redemptions paid fell from USD 721.9 million in FY2024 to USD 130.4 million in FY2026, which left cash for debt reduction, but the company intends USD 300.0 million in fiscal 2027, USD 150.0 million of patronage cash and up to USD 150.0 million of redemptions, beside USD 168.7 million of preferred dividends a year.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The case for lower governance risk is strong. Members own the business and are also its customers and suppliers, total equities of USD 11,644.8 million are 57.90% of assets, and USD 6,256.0 million of patron equity certificates can be redeemed only when the board decides, which cushions creditors in a downturn and was used in FY2026 when payouts were cut. The view would move to higher risk if fiscal 2027 redemptions exceed the USD 150.0 million intended, if CF Nitrogen distributions fall below USD 447.3 million while capital spending rises, or if losses emerge in the CHS Capital book; it would move to lower risk if the debt agreements show distribution limits that bind the board.
Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 144; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 169–170; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 158; calculation A06
### Limitations
- The number of members and the split of voting power between individual and cooperative members are not stated, so how concentrated control is among members is not established.

- Executed debt agreements are not in the sources, so whether the board can raise distributions without lender consent is not established and the governance view rests on the board's stated policy alone.
- No source states CHS's share of the phosphate venture cost or how the soybean plant and the venture will be funded, so their effect on borrowing is not established.
- The CHS Capital loan book is described only by no significant past-due amounts and an immaterial allowance, so the loss exposure behind that statement is not established.
- Related-party credit to directors is disclosed for one fiscal year, so a longer pattern is not established.

### Transaction summary and new debt issues

CHS announced no merger, sponsor transaction or acquisition in the filings for FY2026. It finished its exit from the Producer Ag joint venture on December 31, 2025, taking working capital, mainly inventory and cash, for its equity interest and amounts previously owed, with no effect on the FY2026 income statement. In FY2025 it paid USD 237.2 million for business acquisitions, and the annual report ties goodwill of USD 59.5 million that year to the acquisition of West Central Ag Services.

No new note issue appears for FY2026. The USD 80.0 million of notes due in fiscal 2026 were repaid, leaving private placement notes at USD 1,703.0 million. The new term debt was a USD 300.0 million draw on the revolving term facility between November 30, 2025 and February 28, 2026, which reverts to a nonrevolving term loan payable October 29, 2029, and amendments on August 26, 2026 extended the securitization and repurchase facilities to August 25, 2027.

Two growth projects are announced but not yet approved: a USD 700 million soybean plant in Wisconsin and a USD 450 million phosphate joint venture with OCP North America in Louisiana, both expected in late 2028 or 2029. The company intends USD 300.0 million of fiscal 2027 patronage cash and equity redemptions; none of these is a completed transaction, and no funding plan is stated.

spans.text: # CP-2 Fundamental credit for CHS INC (chscp), as of 2026-11-05
## Request

Fundamental credit view of CHS INC (issuer id chscp), as of 2026-11-05, on the credit_snapshot pathway. Scope: a creditor's synthesis of business risk, earnings durability, liquidity, leverage, refinancing and financial policy from the seven supplied filings and releases and the three earlier analyses, with no rating, security recommendation or sizing.
## Sources

## Findings
### Bottom line

CHS has a strong year-end credit profile, with net debt at 1.14x EBITDA and USD 3,063.6 million of cash and undrawn revolver, but its earnings are cyclical and policy-dependent, and seasonal debt, rising capital spending and higher member payouts can erode that cushion.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation B01; calculation B05

The main downside path is a refining-margin and farm-economy downturn that meets peak-season borrowing while payouts and capital spending rise: on FY2025-level EBITDA and the fiscal 2027 plan, net debt would reach about USD 4,604.8 million at the peak, 3.26x. Covenant levels, ratings and debt agreements are not in the filings, so headroom is not established.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation B08; calculation B09; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 163
### Key findings

- Year-end credit metrics are strong and improving. Net debt was 1.14x EBITDA against 1.88x a year earlier, EBITDA covered cash interest 11.79x against 9.57x, and total debt fell from USD 2,988.3 million to USD 2,501.7 million as working capital released cash. Creditors are well covered on the 2026 year-end balance sheet.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation B01; calculation B02; calculation B03

- The year end is the seasonal low for debt, so leverage through the year is higher. Net debt was USD 3,879.3 million at the February 28, 2026 quarter end, 1.73 times the year-end level, and the securitization and repurchase facilities were used to USD 850.0 million and USD 250.0 million at quarter ends; both run only to August 25, 2027, so receivables funding is a recurring renewal exposure.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-Q_2026-02-28_chscp-20260228.htm.jsonl, pages 12–13; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 164; calculation B04; calculation B14

- Earnings quality is lower than the ratios suggest because 28.9% of EBITDA is equity income and CF Nitrogen alone supplied 36.0% of pre-tax earnings. Distributions exceeded equity income by USD 25.4 million in FY2026, so the income was cash-backed, but it follows urea and UAN prices and the interest is a 7.86% stake CHS cannot control.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 158; calculation B06

- The swing factor is Energy, where policy decides part of the margin. Energy earned USD 554.6 million before tax against a USD 19.0 million loss in FY2025, helped by about USD 205.0 million of small refinery exemption relief; a repeat of the FY2025 margin would remove most of the FY2026 earnings uplift.

- Liquidity is adequate on committed lines and the maturity profile is gentle. Cash of USD 263.6 million sits beside an undrawn USD 2,800.0 million revolver that expires April 21, 2028; the notes are USD 1,703.0 million of unsecured private placements and a USD 300.0 million term loan, with USD 450.0 million due in fiscal 2030 the largest scheduled year. Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 163–165; calculation B05; calculation B13

The fiscal 2027 plan absorbs USD 1,361.3 million of capital spending, major maintenance, preferred dividends and member payouts, which FY2026 operating cash flow of USD 1,584.0 million covers by USD 222.7 million but FY2025 operating cash flow of USD 635.8 million would miss by USD 725.5 million; the board can cut payouts but has just signalled a rise.

### Contrary evidence and what would change the view

The strongest evidence against a cautious reading is that even the downside case leaves net debt at 3.26x EBITDA at the seasonal peak, committed lines of USD 2,800.0 million exceed the USD 725.5 million of extra borrowing it needs, and member equity of USD 11,644.8 million is 57.90% of assets, so a liquidity break would need a worse outcome than a repeat of FY2025. The view would improve if covenant levels show wide headroom, if period-end debt stays well below the February level, or if Energy earnings prove less dependent on exemptions. It would worsen if the securitization and repurchase facilities are not extended beyond August 25, 2027, if equity distributions from CF Nitrogen fall while capital spending runs at USD 850.8 million, or if payouts exceed the USD 300.0 million intended.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation B09; calculation B15
### Limitations
- No rating, market price or peer data is supplied, so the profile is not placed against comparable high-yield issuers or agency criteria, and the label strong describes CHS's own metrics only.

- The downside case is this module's illustration built from FY2025 operating cash flow and EBITDA and the fiscal 2027 plan, not a calculated stress, so the 3.26x peak figure is indicative and ignores timing within the year.
- Debt is known only at five period ends, so the true intra-quarter peak is not established and the USD 4,604.8 million downside peak may understate the borrowing need.
- The sources give no forecast beyond the fiscal 2027 intentions, so the outlook beyond twelve months is qualitative and the fiscal 2028 effect of the new plants is not established.

### Strengths and weaknesses

CHS's main strengths are financial, not competitive. Low year-end leverage and high interest cover let it absorb one weak year without refinancing pressure, as net debt of 1.14x EBITDA and cover of 11.79x show. A USD 2,800.0 million undrawn committed revolver and a long-dated unsecured note stack mean no large maturity wall, with USD 450.0 million the largest year. Member equity of 57.90% of assets and board-discretionary redemption of equity certificates give a buffer. Scale, with USD 39.2 billion of revenue across energy, grains and crop inputs, spreads exposure across three commodity chains. Finally, there is no sponsor, so value extraction by an owner is not a documented risk.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 144; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 163–165; calculation B01; calculation B05; calculation B13

Its main weaknesses are earnings volatility and seasonal reliance on short-term funding. Gross margin is thin at 4.56% of revenue and operating margin only 1.51%, so a small price or volume move changes earnings sharply. Half of pre-tax earnings is equity income from joint ventures CHS does not control, led by CF Nitrogen. Energy earnings depend on refining margins, renewable energy credit costs and refinery exemptions that may not recur. Seasonal borrowing lifts net debt to 1.73 times its year-end level, funded partly by receivables facilities that need renewal by August 2027. Capital spending and member payouts are both set to rise while farm demand is weak, and covenant levels are unknown.

### Company description and group structure

CHS is a farmer-owned cooperative whose three reportable segments run on commodity spreads. Energy refines about 190,000 barrels a day at Laurel and McPherson, Grains is the largest cooperative marketer and processor of grain and oilseeds, and Agronomy sells crop inputs and holds a 7.86% interest in CF Nitrogen. Revenue is price-driven and thin-margin, so the cash that services debt comes from refining spreads, processing margins and joint venture distributions, not from revenue scale. Grains is 55.02% of revenue but 11.29% of pre-tax earnings, while Energy is 28.96% of revenue and 49.13% of earnings.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 4–5; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 67

No sponsor, parent or restricted group sits above the issuer. Control rests with member-elected farmer directors, preferred holders and lenders have no vote, and the debt is issued by the consolidated cooperative; CHS Capital, Cofina Funding and the equity-method joint ventures sit below it. For creditors this removes sponsor extraction risk but leaves the board's discretionary payout policy as the financial-policy lever, and the structural position of unsecured notes against receivables-backed financing is not established because no debt agreement is supplied.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 91; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 164
### Revenue drivers, cost structure and cash conversion

Revenue is volatile through price and stable through volume. Revenue fell 9.68% in FY2025 and rose 10.63% in FY2026 on commodity prices while volumes moved less, and the company states it is exposed to weather, trade policy and the farm economy. Because gross margin is only 3.21% to 4.56% of revenue, creditors should read revenue as a driver of working capital, not of earnings.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); EX-99.1_2026-11-04_a4qfy26earningrelease.htm.jsonl, page 1; calculation B11

Costs are largely variable commodity inputs, with fixed refinery and processing costs behind them, so margin depends on spreads. Operating margin was 0.26% in FY2025 and 1.51% in FY2026; marketing, general and administrative expense rose 14.3% in FY2026 on incentive pay and software amortisation. This is operating leverage to spreads: refining margin, crush margin and urea prices explain most year-to-year change, which makes margin resilience weak without an offset from equity income.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 72; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 66

Cash conversion swings with working capital and capital spending. Free cash flow after capital spending and major maintenance was USD 1,052.5 million in FY2026, minus USD 364.2 million in FY2025 and USD 441.4 million in FY2024, and Q4 of FY2026 delivered USD 1,382.8 million of operating cash flow as receivables unwound. Capital spending flexes, since major maintenance fell from USD 271.4 million to USD 68.3 million, but FY2027 plans USD 850.8 million, so conversion in a weak year is the credit test.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); calculation B12; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 76; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 146
### Competitive forces and policy environment

Rivalry and buyer power cap pricing. CHS competes with larger, better known companies, its members are not obliged to trade with it, and consolidation among cooperative customers and input manufacturers could remove it from supply chains. Substitution matters mainly to Energy, where lower fuel demand would hit diesel sold to farms. These forces explain why margins are thin and why creditors should not extrapolate FY2026 spreads, but they also spread risk across many customers, none above 10% of receivables.

Policy is a material credit driver here. The EPA's March 2026 renewable volume obligation is the highest ever, renewable credit prices rose 86% and 82%, and the small refinery exemptions that gave about USD 205.0 million of relief in FY2026 depend on petitions CHS may not win again; tax rules for cooperatives and clean fuel credits add further policy sensitivity, and China's 2025 suspension of soybean imports shows trade exposure. These factors can move Energy and Grains earnings by more than the cost of CHS's interest, so they belong in the primary downside path.
Basis: Business & governance (CP-1A); 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 46; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 63–64; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 168
### SWOT in credit terms

Strengths: low year-end leverage, large unsecured term debt with no large maturity wall, USD 2,800.0 million of undrawn committed revolver, member equity buffer and board-controlled payouts. Weaknesses: thin margins, half of pre-tax earnings from joint ventures, policy-dependent Energy earnings, seasonal debt and unknown covenants. Opportunities: the Wisconsin soybean plant and phosphate venture could add earnings from late 2028 or 2029 if approved and funded sensibly, and lower major maintenance in fiscal 2027 helps cash. Threats: a repeat of FY2025 margins, loss of CF Nitrogen distributions, non-renewal of the receivables facilities by August 2027, farm credit losses at CHS Capital, and tax or exemption changes.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); EX-99.1_2026-11-04_a4qfy26earningrelease.htm.jsonl, page 2; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 76; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 163–165
### Financial profile and credit quality

Scale and market position are strong: revenue of USD 39.2 billion and a leading cooperative position in energy and grains. Competitive advantage is average, resting on member relationships and owned logistics rather than pricing power. Business diversification is average because three chains are diversified but equity income concentrates earnings in one joint venture. Cost and capex flexibility is average, since payouts and growth capital are discretionary while refineries need turnarounds. Margin stability is weak, with gross margin at 3.21% in FY2025 and 4.56% in FY2026. Free cash flow stability is average, from minus USD 364.2 million to USD 1,052.5 million. Ability to refinance is average: long-dated unsecured notes show private market access, but no rating or market data is supplied and the receivables lines renew in 2027. Liquidity is strong at the year end with USD 3,063.6 million of cash and undrawn revolver, subject to unstated letters of credit. Financial policy and governance is average: no sponsor and board control support creditors, but payouts are discretionary and covenants are unseen.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation B05; calculation B11; calculation B12

The main support is year-end leverage of 1.27x total debt to EBITDA and cover of 11.79x; the main constraints are earnings concentration and seasonal debt; the trend is better in FY2026 than FY2025 but cyclical; and the key missing datapoints are covenant levels, ratings and debt agreements.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Source readiness (CP-0)
### Outlook, tailwinds and headwinds

Over twelve to twenty-four months, tailwinds are the company's FY2026 operating cash flow, lower major maintenance of USD 41.8 million, higher crush margins from biofuel policy and CF Nitrogen pricing, while headwinds are weak farm demand, record renewable credit costs, a possible end to exemptions and capital spending of USD 850.8 million. Over three to five years the Wisconsin soybean plant and phosphate venture add capacity from late 2028 or 2029 but raise capital needs first; none of the filings gives a forecast, so the medium-term outlook is qualitative.

Basis: 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 62–64; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 69; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 76; EX-99.1_2026-11-04_a4qfy26earningrelease.htm.jsonl, pages 1–2
### Downside scenario

The downside is a repeat of FY2025 conditions at peak-season borrowing under the fiscal 2027 plan. The initiating condition is Energy margins falling back as crack spreads and exemptions normalise while farmers defer purchases and trade restrictions persist. The first operating break is Energy and Agronomy earnings; operating cash flow falls to the FY2025 level of USD 635.8 million against USD 1,361.3 million of planned capital spending, major maintenance, preferred dividends and member payouts, a shortfall of USD 725.5 million that is funded by borrowing. Net debt would then be about USD 2,963.6 million at year end, 2.10x FY2025-level EBITDA of USD 1,412.3 million, and about USD 4,604.8 million at the seasonal peak, 3.26x. The revolver of USD 2,800.0 million exceeds the extra borrowing, so liquidity would hold, and the observable triggers are covenant tests, the August 2027 receivables renewal and the April 2028 revolver expiry. Management levers are lower payouts and capital spending, which the board has used before.

Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); calculation B08; calculation B09; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, page 76; 10-K_2026-08-31_chscp-20260831.htm.jsonl, pages 163–164
### Overall credit view

Overall, CHS presents a strong business profile on scale and a cooperative structure with no sponsor, but credit quality is constrained by thin and policy-dependent margins, half of pre-tax earnings from joint ventures and seasonal debt that is far above the year-end level. Cash-flow durability appears adequate: cover is high in a good year but free cash flow was negative in FY2025. Refinancing capacity is likely to depend on renewing the receivables facilities by August 2027 and the revolver by April 2028 and on covenant headroom that the filings do not show. The primary downside path is a margin downturn that meets peak-season borrowing while payouts and capital spending rise. Further analysis would require the credit agreement, covenant levels, ratings and CHS Capital loan data. Fundamental credit completed. Top risk: policy-dependent Energy margins meeting peak-season borrowing.
Basis: Financial foundation (CP-1); Business & governance (CP-1A); Source readiness (CP-0)
